summary: Psalm 149 calls the assembly of Israel to praise Yahweh with a new song, dance, tambourine, and harp. It grounds that praise in Yahweh’s delight in his people and his crowning of the humble with salvation. The final lines join praise with judgment language, picturing the saints with high praises in their mouths and a sword in their hand.
whyItMatters: This psalm stands near the end of Psalms, where the collection moves into repeated calls to praise. It also shows that final praise in the Psalter can include hard language about justice and judgment, not only celebration.

context.author: No individual author is named in the psalm. Psalms as a whole is an anthology with many writers and collections.
context.audience: Israel’s worshiping and instructed community, later received by Jewish and Christian communities for public and private prayer.
context.date: The Psalms contain material from different periods and were gathered into a later five-book collection; the chapter does not identify its date of composition.
context.setting: Book V of Psalms, in the final praise sequence near the close of the Hebrew Psalter.
context.literaryForm: Hebrew poetry and communal praise, using summons, parallel lines, instruments, and vivid judgment imagery.

outline.heading: A New Song in the Assembly
outline.note: The psalm opens with a command to praise Yahweh and sing in the assembly of the saints.

outline.heading: Joy in Maker and King
outline.note: Israel and the children of Zion are called to rejoice, dance, and sing with tambourine and harp.

outline.heading: Yahweh’s Pleasure in His People
outline.note: The reason for praise is Yahweh’s favor: he takes pleasure in his people, crowns the humble with salvation, and gives the saints joy and honor.

outline.heading: Praise and Sword
outline.note: The psalm pictures high praises in the mouth and a two-edged sword in the hand, with judgment on nations, peoples, kings, and nobles.

outline.heading: Written Judgment and Final Praise
outline.note: The closing line speaks of executing the written judgment, calls this an honor for the saints, and ends with praise.

keyVerses.text: Praise Yahweh! Sing to Yahweh a new song, his praise in the assembly of the saints.
keyVerses.why: This opening gives the psalm its setting and action: communal praise directed to Yahweh.

keyVerses.text: For Yahweh takes pleasure in his people. He crowns the humble with salvation.
keyVerses.why: This verse gives the reason for the praise: Yahweh’s delight in his people and his saving honor for the humble.

keyVerses.text: May the high praises of God be in their mouths, and a two-edged sword in their hand,
keyVerses.why: This verse marks the psalm’s sharp turn from celebration to judgment imagery.

keyVerses.text: to execute on them the written judgment. All his saints have this honor. Praise Yah!
keyVerses.why: The final verse completes the judgment sequence and closes the psalm with praise.

themes: joy in Israel’s Maker and King

questions.question: Who is being called to praise in this psalm?
questions.answer: The psalm names Israel, the children of Zion, and the saints. It is written as a communal summons rather than a private meditation. The praise happens in an assembly and also reaches the more intimate image of singing on beds.

questions.question: What does “new song” mean here?
questions.answer: The chapter does not explain the phrase beyond commanding it. Within this psalm, the “new song” is praise to Yahweh in the assembly, connected with rejoicing, music, and Yahweh’s favor toward his people. The phrase should not be pressed into a specific occasion that the chapter itself does not name.

questions.question: Why does verse 2 call God both maker and King?
questions.answer: Verse 2 says Israel should rejoice in “him who made them” and that the children of Zion should be joyful “in their King.” The psalm presents Yahweh as both the one responsible for the people’s existence and the ruler in whom they rejoice. It does not pause to explain the titles; it uses them as reasons for praise.

questions.question: Are dance and instruments part of the praise here?
questions.answer: Yes. Verse 3 explicitly names dance, tambourine, and harp as part of praising Yahweh’s name. The chapter depicts embodied and musical praise, not only spoken words.

questions.question: What does it mean that Yahweh “crowns the humble with salvation”?
questions.answer: The psalm says Yahweh takes pleasure in his people and crowns the humble with salvation. The image links lowliness with honor given by God. The chapter does not define the form of salvation in detail, so it is safest to say that the humble are pictured as honored by Yahweh’s saving action.

questions.question: Why are the saints singing “on their beds”?
questions.answer: Verse 5 says the saints rejoice in honor and sing for joy on their beds. The line extends praise beyond the public assembly into a private or resting place. The psalm does not specify whether this is nighttime praise, security after rescue, or another setting, so readers should avoid making one setting certain.

questions.question: Why does a praise psalm mention a two-edged sword?
questions.answer: Verses 6-9 join praise with judgment language: high praises are in the saints’ mouths, and a two-edged sword is in their hand. Readers differ on how to understand this imagery, with some reading it as a concrete battle scene and others as poetic or liturgical language about God’s judgment. The chapter itself presents the judgment as “written” and as an honor given to the saints, but it does not give a historical battle setting.

questions.question: Does this psalm authorize personal revenge?
questions.answer: The chapter speaks of executing vengeance and punishments, binding kings and nobles, and carrying out written judgment. It presents this as part of the saints’ honor within a communal praise psalm, not as a private person’s permission to settle grudges. Because the psalm gives no direct modern application, responsible readers should keep the historical and poetic distance in view.

questions.question: What is the “written judgment”?
questions.answer: Verse 9 says the saints execute “the written judgment,” but the chapter does not identify a specific document or passage. The phrase suggests judgment already determined or recorded, but the psalm itself does not say more. Interpreters debate whether this points to earlier covenant or judgment traditions, a royal-war setting, or a poetic way of saying God’s judgment is established.

glossary.def: The gathered community in which Yahweh’s praise is sung in verse 1.
The people named in verses 1, 5, and 9 as the worshiping group who praise and receive honor.
A phrase in verse 2 for the people called to be joyful in their King.
An instrument named in verse 3 as part of the psalm’s musical praise.
The weapon named in verse 6 as the psalm turns from praise language to judgment imagery.
